claims.text: TaVCrW is initially a disordered BCC solid solution at 0 K.
W-Ta-Cr-V alloys can exhibit Cr-V-rich segregation and short-range order.
Replacing EAM and thermodynamic integration with an MTP-FEP workflow will reduce computational cost by more than 80%.
The MTP-FEP workflow will maintain a free-energy accuracy of 0.5 meV/atom relative to TOR-TILD.
Solid-phase SRO stabilizes TaVCrW by approximately 2-3 meV/atom.
Electronic gap effects in the liquid can shift the melting temperature by tens of kelvin.
A supercell containing more than 200 atoms is sufficient to capture SRO correlations and resolve a 2-3 meV/atom stabilization energy.
The SRO contribution should be validated over 2000-2400 K.
Accurate reproduction of the ab initio phase-space distribution, including local environments and Warren-Cowley SRO parameters, is critical for FEP convergence.
An MTP trained on solid and liquid DFT configurations can approximate the TaVCrW potential-energy surface with sub-meV accuracy.
Accurate MTP phase-space sampling allows FEP to determine solid-liquid free-energy differences without a thermodynamic-integration path.
Failure to resolve the 2-3 meV/atom SRO stabilization will produce errors in the predicted melting point.
Including high-temperature liquid configurations in the MTP training set implicitly captures electronic gap effects.
The TaVCrW melting result will agree with TOR-TILD within approximately 10-20 K.
The standard EAM-based TOR-TILD thermodynamic-integration workflow is computationally expensive.
Empirical GGA-PBE/LDA underbinding and overbinding rules fail for V and Cr at 0 K and may propagate errors into MTP training.
Non-magnetic DFT training may omit high-temperature magnetic fluctuations relevant to TaVCrW.
Neglected magnetic entropy could cause liquid free-energy errors exceeding 0.5 meV/atom.
The method is falsified if its benchmark free-energy difference from TOR-TILD exceeds 0.5 meV/atom or its computational-cost reduction is less than 80%.
